how-much-should-i-charge-to-rent-out-equ.text:
← Equipment rental break-even calculator

How much should I charge to rent out equipment?

The common answer is to look up what the branch down the road charges for the same machine and shade it. That sets your price from someone else's cost base, someone else's finance deal, and — the part nobody publishes — someone else's utilization. A rate that works for a depot renting the same excavator 18 days a month can be underwater for an owner renting it 7.

Open the free rental break-even calculator

The number that actually sets the rate

Utilization. Ownership cost does not pause when the asset is in the yard. Finance or depreciation, insurance, storage, licensing and scheduled servicing accrue for the whole month, and only the billable days can carry them. Divide monthly ownership cost by expected billable days — not by 30 — and you have the ownership recovery each day has to earn.

That single division is why a purchase-price rule of thumb misleads. Two operators can pay the same for the same machine and need genuinely different rates.

What the day rate has to cover

CostBehaves like
Finance or depreciation, insurance, storage, licensing, scheduled servicingMonthly, whether or not it goes out — recovered across billable days only
Delivery and collectionPer booking, and often per booking regardless of hire length
Cleaning and turnaroundPer booking, and it consumes a day you cannot rebill
Fuel, consumables, wear partsPer day or per hour of use
Damage and loss reserveA percentage you set — cheaper than discovering the average the hard way

Delivery and cleaning are the two most often left out, because they feel like overhead rather than part of the hire. On short bookings they frequently exceed the ownership recovery for the same booking.

A rate you can defend

  1. Total the asset's monthly ownership cost.
  2. Divide by the billable days you honestly expect in a month — last season's number, not the optimistic one.
  3. Add this booking's delivery, collection, cleaning, consumables and damage reserve.
  4. That sum is the break-even day rate. Below it the booking loses money.
  5. Add the margin you intend to keep, and quote from there.

The calculator runs that arithmetic in your browser and shows the contribution a proposed price leaves after variable costs, plus the monthly utilization the asset needs to recover its ownership cost at that price. You can download a plain-text snapshot of the quote for your own records.

Worked example

An asset costing $1,800 a month to own, rented at 8 billable days a month, carries $225 a day of ownership recovery before anything else happens. Add $90 of delivery and collection, half a day of cleaning, and a damage reserve, and a "competitive" $200 day rate is losing money on every booking — while the same machine at 16 billable days carries $112.50 of ownership recovery and the same $200 looks entirely different. Nothing about the machine changed. Only the utilization did.

Common questions

How much should I charge to rent out equipment?

Start from what the asset costs you to own for a month — finance or depreciation, insurance, storage, licensing, scheduled maintenance — then divide that by the number of billable days you actually expect, not by 30. Add the variable cost of the individual booking: delivery and collection, cleaning and turnaround, fuel or consumables, and a damage reserve. The day rate has to cover both, plus the margin you intend to keep.

Why does utilization matter more than the purchase price?

Ownership cost accrues every day of the month whether the asset is out or sitting in the yard. If a machine bills 8 days a month, those 8 days carry all 30 days of ownership cost. The same machine at 16 billable days carries half as much per day. Two operators with an identical purchase price and identical financing can have day rates that differ by a factor of two purely because of utilization, which is why copying a competitor's published rate is not a pricing method.

Is a break-even rate the same as the price I should quote?

No. Break-even is the floor — the number below which the booking loses money once ownership recovery and the booking's own variable costs are counted. The quoted price is a commercial decision above that floor. The value of knowing the floor is that you can discount deliberately, and stop, rather than discovering after the season that a busy year did not pay for the asset.

No warranty. This free page is not financial, tax, legal, insurance, or engineering advice, and it does not tell you what to charge or whether an asset is worth owning. Utilization, residual value, and damage frequency are assumptions you supply, and a wrong assumption produces a wrong rate. Verify every figure against your own accounts and a qualified professional before relying on it or quoting a customer. index.html.text:
A private pricing tool for independent rental operators

Price the booking, not just the day rate.

Find the booking price and monthly utilization your equipment needs after ownership, delivery, cleaning, damage reserve, and idle time are counted.

Booking assumptions

How to use the result

The minimum booking price recovers the asset's allocated ownership cost plus booking-specific costs. Break-even bookings per month is how many of this booking it takes to cover monthly ownership at this contribution; the day-share row is those bookings times rental days, divided by available days. These are arithmetic scenarios, not a guarantee of profit, and they are not a recommended price.

Common questions

Why is the minimum price sometimes higher than the target-margin price, and sometimes lower?

They are built from different pieces. The minimum price recovers booking-specific costs, this booking's ownership cost, and this booking's share of your monthly fixed overhead — on the defaults, $77 booking costs + $26.67 ownership + $7.50 of amortized monthly overhead = $111.17. The target-margin price applies your target margin to booking costs and ownership only, with no monthly-overhead add-on: $103.67 marked up to a 35% margin is $159.49. On the defaults the margin price wins, but a low margin target paired with a large per-booking share of monthly overhead can flip that. Always quote at least the higher of the two.

How does the asset's purchase price turn into a per-day cost?

Purchase cost divided by recovery life in rental days, then multiplied by the days this booking uses. On the defaults, a $2,400 asset with a 180-rental-day recovery life is $13.33 a day, so a 2-day booking carries $26.67 of ownership cost. A shorter recovery life — expecting to replace or overhaul the asset sooner — raises this number for every booking, not just long ones.

What does “break-even bookings per month” actually count?

How many bookings like this one, in a month, it takes for their contribution (booking price minus booking-specific costs and this booking's own ownership-cost share) to cover your monthly fixed overhead. On the defaults that is $75 fixed overhead ÷ $76.33 contribution ≈ 0.98 — just under one booking a month covers the fixed side. The day-share row turns that into a percentage of your available rental days (0.98 bookings × 2 days ÷ 20 available days ≈ 9.8%), so you can see how much of the month's capacity break-even actually consumes. A booking whose contribution is zero or negative never breaks even at any volume, however small fixed overhead is — see the next question.

What does it mean if my contribution is negative?

The booking price does not even cover its own booking-specific costs and ownership share before monthly fixed overhead is counted at all — every booking at that price loses money outright, and no amount of volume fixes it. Raise the price, cut booking-specific costs, or shorten the rental days before accepting bookings at that number.

Can I use this for more than one type of booking or asset?

Run each one separately. Rental days, delivery/cleaning/damage costs, and ownership recovery all differ by booking length and asset, so a single run only describes the scenario you typed in. Save a draft for each booking type you quote regularly rather than averaging them into one number.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — everything runs in your browser. Saved drafts live in this browser's local storage, the downloaded quote snapshot is a plain-text file you keep yourself, and “Copy share link” encodes the same booking fields into the page's own URL fragment (never sent to a server) so you can hand a live, editable scenario to a partner or customer. Anonymous feature counts are local-only and optional; the button above turns them off.

Two different shapes: Booqable runs your whole rental operation — inventory, online booking, checkout scanning, invoicing — as an ongoing subscription account. What each tool is for

Booqable is rental and inventory management software, sold under an ongoing subscription account to operators running a real fleet of rentable equipment. It tracks every asset's availability across your inventory, runs an online booking storefront customers can reserve from directly, checks equipment out and back in with barcode or QR scanning, and generates quotes, contracts, and invoices, all synced across staff and locations. Setting it up means creating an account, importing your inventory, and configuring a storefront and checkout workflow — not a one-off calculation. Booqable's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, feature tiers, or pricing, so only its well-documented category and identity are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

vs-flat-day-rate.html.text:
← Equipment Rental Break-Even Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat day rate

A flat day rate — one round number for every booking of an asset — is the fastest way to quote a rental, and for bookings that rarely vary it can work fine. It stops working the moment delivery distance, cleaning effort, damage risk, or rental length changes from booking to booking, because none of that is priced separately in a single number.

What each one is for

A flat day rate is quick to quote and easy for a customer to compare against a competitor's number. What it does not do is separate the price into anything an operator can check against a specific booking — it does not scale with delivery distance or damage risk, it has no ownership-recovery logic built in, and it cannot tell you whether the rate actually covers the asset's per-day ownership cost or your monthly fixed overhead at your real booking volume.

This calculator takes one proposed booking — price, rental days, delivery, cleaning, and damage-reserve costs, plus the asset's purchase cost and recovery life — and works out the booking-specific costs, the per-day ownership cost, the minimum price that recovers ownership and your monthly fixed overhead, the price that hits a target contribution margin, and how many bookings like this one it takes each month to break even. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and nothing you type is uploaded.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What do I charge for a typical, low-variation booking?Either one — a flat rate is fine if delivery, cleaning, and damage risk rarely change.
What does an unusually far, dirty, or high-risk booking actually cost?This calculator — it prices this booking's own delivery, cleaning, and damage-reserve figures, not an average.
Does my rate cover this asset's ownership cost and my monthly overhead?This calculator's minimum price and break-even figures, not a flat rate — a round number tracks neither.
How many bookings like this one do I need each month to break even?This calculator's break-even-bookings and day-share figures.
How much should I charge to rent out this equipment?This calculator's worked walkthrough.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Most rental operators get different value from each: a flat day rate for a quick quote on a booking that looks like every other one, and this calculator for the booking that does not — a longer delivery, a messier turnaround, a higher damage risk, or simply checking that the round number you have been quoting still covers ownership and overhead at your current volume.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Nothing you type is uploaded.

Common questions

What is a flat day rate, and why do rental operators use it?

One round number charged for every booking of a given asset, regardless of how far it is delivered, how much cleaning or turnaround it needs, or how much damage-reserve risk it carries. It is fast to quote and easy for a customer to compare, which is why many small operators start there, especially early on when bookings are simple and similar.

What does a flat rate hide as bookings get more varied?

The price stays the same while the costs behind it do not. A flat rate sized for a short local booking under-prices one with a long delivery, heavy cleaning, or a higher damage risk, and over-prices a simple one — and it says nothing about whether the rate actually recovers the asset's ownership cost or your monthly fixed overhead at all.

Can a flat rate tell me how many bookings I need to break even?

No. A flat rate is a price, not a break-even calculation. Whether a given rate covers your monthly fixed overhead depends on the asset's ownership cost per day, the booking-specific costs on top, and how many bookings like it you run in a month — none of which a single number tracks. A rate can look reasonable and still lose money at your actual volume.

Does a flat rate separate ownership cost from booking-specific costs?

Only if the operator works it out by hand every time. A flat rate bundles delivery, cleaning, damage reserve, and the asset's per-day ownership cost into one number, so raising or lowering it does not say which piece is under-covered, or whether a longer or shorter rental should carry a different figure.

Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is uploaded.
